articles.text: After 17 years in business, Piedmont Auto Care, the Shell station at the corner of Wildwood and Grand Avenue, is closing its doors. Earlier this week, owner Jeff Hansen sold the station and the property to Shell Recharge, a division of the Shell corporation that specializes in EV charging stations. It would potentially be the first of its kind in the U.S. The Shell station has been in Piedmont for 95 years. Hansen said the decision was motivated by the cost of upcoming and necessary renovations to the property as well as his predictions of the future of the auto industry. “We have three 10,000 gallon gas tanks under our pumps that need to be replaced by 2025,” Hansen said. “That’s expensive, but not out of the question as far as maintenance goes.” The installation of new gas tanks under the property would have allowed the station to continue pumping fuel for decades. “But I don’t see people pumping more and more gas in the future,” he explained. Hansen has been watching electric vehicle sales climb steadily since 2010. He believes that in the near future electric vehicles will become far more common. “It doesn’t make a lot of sense to replace those tanks if that’s the situation. I’ve always been looking at trends, and this generation’s trend is electric vehicles.” Hansen will physically vacate the premises by the end of November, but all auto service has ceased and his mechanics will be working at other nearby stations. articles.text: Thanksgiving is approaching quickly and with it comes the time-honored tradition of the Piedmont Turkey Trot. On Thanksgiving morning, Thursday, November 23, at 8:30 a.m. an estimated 2,400 runners will hit the streets with running shoes, bibs, and water bottles to deliver a pre-emptive strike against those Thanksgiving calories. The Turkey Trot is a 5K course (3.1 miles) on city streets intended for all runners, joggers and dog walkers, young and old, casual and experienced. “The Piedmont Turkey Trot is a much-loved community event that raises funds for the high school cross-country and track and field team, as well as the Boosters,” said Race Director Sydney Proctor. articles.text: The City of Piedmont has published a Draft Environmental Impact Report (Draft EIR) for the implementation of the City’s 6th Cycle Housing Element for public review and comment. Community members may submit written comments on the Draft EIR to Planning Director Kevin Jackson through December 18 at 5 p.m. The Draft EIR studies the impacts of Housing Element implementation as a whole – looking at the overall impacts to Piedmont once each of the 77 programs included in the Housing Element are realized. For each impact identified, the Draft EIR assesses how significant it would be and lists steps the City would take to mitigate that impact, where possible. Community members may view the Draft EIR in person at Piedmont City Hall or online at piedmontishome.org. After December 18, staff will respond to comments received. The Planning Commission and City Council will then consider the EIR at public hearings, likely in early 2024.

articles.text: Last year Piedmont elementary school students took part in Ruby Bridges Walk to School Day, a nationwide event, for the first time. On Tuesday, November 14, the event will be expanded city-wide, inciting all students and community members to honor Ruby Bridges and her courageous message of kindness, inclusion and activism. In 1960, the courage of a sixyear-old student in New Orleans was on display every day as Ruby Bridges was the first Black student to attend an all-white school in New Orleans. She broke the segregation barrier every day, walking past a screaming mob under guard of federal marshals. In 2018, fifth graders in South San Francisco took inspiration from Ruby’s courage and advocated to make November 14, Ruby Bridges Day. San Mateo County Office of Education later made their dream a reality, and ever since schools nationwide have been following suit. In September 2021, the California State Senate passed a resolution proclaiming November 14 as Ruby Bridges Walk to School Day. Last year over 90,000 kids in 36 states, including California, participated. “Even though it can feel like Piedmont exists in a bubble, untouched from the issues Ruby Bridges was fighting for (desegregation, racial equity), that is simply not the case,” said PHS sophomore Meher Bachher, “Ruby Bridges’ actions and her teachings prove to us in our own community that no matter our age, we can accomplish incredible feats if we have the dedication.” 7:45 a.m.: Pathways of Kindness. Piedmont High School Affinity Mentors at Piedmont Park will create “Pathways of Kindness” with chalk in the city center. Create a bouquet of diversity, talk bubbles with important messages, rainbows of all colors, and other artistic expressions of “everyone is welcome and belongs.” 8:05 a.m.: The Ruby Bridges Pledge Piedmont Affinity Mentors speak about Ruby Bridges and her message. Take the Ruby Bridges Pledge together. 8:10 a.m.: Prepare to walk to school Learn the history, grab some cool Ruby Bridges swag and walk to school in unity on November 14.

articles.text: Curiosity drives human progress, yet modern life often stifles our innate sense of wonder. As Albert Einstein once said, “I have no special talent. I am only passionately curious.” Children are bursting with curiosity, eagerly investigating the world around them. But busy schedules, screens and standardized education can dampen inquisitive young minds. The good news is that parents can take steps to keep their child’s curiosity alive. 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. Allow unstructured free time for open-ended play and exploration. Don’t overschedule activities. a. Set aside 30-60 minutes per day for unscheduled, non-screen play. b. Allow taking healthy risks outdoors; get into open wilderness and see what happens. c. Go on a “wonder walk” with no set destination. Examine small things up close, like insects and plant buds. Notice patterns and details in nature, architecture, shadows. Provide access to new experiences through travel, museums, nature walks. Exposure sparks questions. a. Visit zoos, aquariums, children’s museums. b. Hike a new trail, swim in a lake, climb a hill. c. Travel whether near or far - explore diverse neighborhoods. Supply games, toys and books that encourage inquiry over predetermined outcomes. a. Use toys like Lego without a kit or instructions b. Find a “loose parts” playground c. Choose books on how things work Model curiosity by sharing your own wonderings and asking imaginative questions. a. Wonder aloud - “Hmm, I wonder how that tradition started?” b. Ask open questions like “What do you think AI will be able to do in two years?” c. Discuss what interests you and what you find fascinating. Embrace mistakes as learning opportunities rather than failures. Praise efforts. a. Emphasize effort over outcomes. Praise trying new things. b. Say “Let’s figure out what went wrong” versus “That’s not right.” c. Share your own mistakes and what you learned. Children love stories. :-) 6. Limit access to devices/information that satisfies all their questions immediately. a. b. c. Set boundaries for recreational screen time. Encourage reading books over quick online searches (experience more long-form inquiry). Withhold constant facts; let them sit with questions. Ask riddles, and work on them for days, or weeks. 7. Ask open-ended questions without easy factual answers. a. What would happen if...? b. c. Do you think there could ever be a rainbow at night? How might you build a car that would keep that person safe? 8. Introduce philosophy by discussing imaginative big questions. a. Do dogs have feelings? b. Is there life on other planets? c. What happens after we die? 9. Help make connections between different fields and ideas. a. Link art, music, math, and science through interdisciplinary projects. b. Compare diverse cultures, time periods, and perspectives. c. Show how seemingly unrelated concepts are connected. 10. Let children sit sometimes with uncertainty instead of answering all questions. a. Tell them it’s okay not to know; model being comfortable with the unknown. b. Admit you don’t have all the answers either. c. Let them research answers when developmentally appropriate. What beauty, understanding and progress lie ahead when curiosity takes flight? The only way to find out is to set it free. Randall Grayson, Ph.D. (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for twenty years. articles.text: 29-26 win vs. Newark includes forcing 6 turnovers in 2nd half Friday night at Newark Memorial marked mission accomplished for Piedmont High’s football team. The Highlanders captured their first Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division title by defeating the Cougars in a heated 29-26 battle on November 3. It marked the first time the school has won a league banner since 2015. “I can’t get over this group of kids. I told you last year when we were struggling how proud I was of us for fighting through games. Once again, we had 17 kids and were down to 16 after an injury. Some people picked us to go 0-10. Nobody knew what we had. We kept telling them to just trust and believe in us, and they did,” said coach Jordan Seiden. It may have not been the most elegant performance after trailing 14-7 at halftime, but Piedmont’s defense responded, forcing six turnovers in the second half, four of which came in the final quarter. Safety Vince Arbit was the game changer with an interception on the first play of the third quarter to change the game’s momentum. “We didn’t get things done in the first half. Coach gave us some inspiring words and reminded us of what we were playing for. I knew we had to come out in the second half and make an impact,” said Arbit. Running back Tommy Ashton was a big part of the victory, recording several bruising runs to set the tone in the second half. As the middle linebacker on defense, he was in the forefront of the defensive turnaround. “Starting the second half, we really turned things up. Linebackers started making tackles, we had three interceptions and really put things together,” he said. Piedmont gained its final lead of 29-26 on a touchdown pass from quarterback Markos Lagios to Sam Shelby with 5:27 left in the game. It was followed by linebacker Brandon Dicke’s fumble recovery and back-to-back interceptions by cornerback Miguel Long “I gave up a touchdown earlier in the game and knew I had to lock in. I anticipated the tip on the first interception and the second was just totally surreal,” said Long. “I saw the quarterback point to the receiver, which made things too easy.” In the fourth quarter Lagios suffered a knee injury with six minutes left but never missed a play. Despite limping back to the huddle, Lagios played on and landed an 80-yard touchdown pass to Shelby for the game winner. PHS now earned the No. 5 seed in the North Coast Section Staff Photos Brandon Dicke had a touchdown reception, an interception, and two fumble recoveries. Game Recap Piedmont started the game strongly with touchdown series capped with Lagios running 14 yards into the end zone for a 7-0 lead after four minutes. However, Newark required just two plays on a long touchdown run by Jovany Morenogutierrez, tying it at 7-7. Newark went ahead 14-7 with 9:47 left in the second quarter. After trading possessions, the Highlanders drove to the Cougar 5-yard-line, but failed to convert on fourth down with 28 seconds left. On Newark’s first play of the second half, Arbit jumped in front of Newark’s receiver for the interception at Newark’s 44. Piedmont then scored on a 20-yard pass down the sideline to Dicke for a 14-14 tie. But the Cougars scored on a bomb to Jaden Lim two minutes later for a 20-14 lead. On Piedmont’s next drive Lagios threw a backwards pass to Shelby, who unloaded a 30-yard pass to Cash Elmquist. Seven plays later, Lagios scored on a 14-yard run, putting Piedmont ahead 21-20. But Piedmont, ever resilient, responded quickly with an injured Lagios threw a pass to Shelby between two defenders down the sideline for an 80-yard touchdown. Shelby scored the 2-point conversion, breaking a tackle on his way to the end zone with 5:27 remaining, and Piedmont held on for the 29-26 victory. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, November 8, 2023 Sports By Jonathan Comeaux Friday night at Newark Memorial marked mission accomplished for Piedmont High’s football team. The Highlanders captured their first Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division title by defeating the Cougars in a heated 29-26 battle on November 3. It marked the first time the school has won a league banner since 2015. “I can’t get over this group of kids. I told you last year when we were struggling how proud I was of us for fighting through games. Once again, we had 17 kids and were down to 16 after an injury. Some people picked us to go 0-10. Nobody knew what we had. We kept telling them to just trust and believe in us, and they did,” said coach Jordan Seiden. It may have not been the most elegant performance after trailing 14-7 at halftime, but Piedmont’s defense responded, forcing six turnovers in the second half, four of which came in the final quarter. Safety Vince Arbit was the game changer with an interception on the first play of the third quarter to change the game’s momentum. “We didn’t get things done in the first half. Coach gave us some inspiring words and reminded us of what we were playing for. I knew we had to come out in the second half and make an impact,” Football team wins first league title since 2015 29-26 win vs. Newark includes forcing 6 turnovers in 2nd half said Arbit. Running back Tommy Ashton was a big part of the victory, recording several bruising runs to set the tone in the second half. As the middle linebacker on defense, he was in the forefront of the defensive turnaround. “Starting the second half, we really turned things up. Linebackers started making tackles, we had three interceptions and really put things together,” he said. Piedmont gained its final lead of 29-26 on a touchdown pass from quarterback Markos Lagios to Sam Shelby with 5:27 left in the game. It was followed by linebacker Brandon Dicke’s fumble recovery and back-to-back interceptions by cornerback Miguel Long “I gave up a touchdown earlier in the game and knew I had to lock in. I anticipated the tip on the first interception and the second was just totally surreal,” said Long. “I saw the quarterback point to the receiver, which made things too easy.” In the fourth quarter Lagios suffered a knee injury with six minutes left but never missed a play. Despite limping back to the huddle, Lagios played on and landed an 80-yard touchdown pass to Shelby for the game winner. On Newark’s first play of the second half, Arbit jumped in front of Newark’s receiver for the interception at Newark’s 44. Shelby scored the 2-point conversion, breaking a tackle on his way to the end zone with 5:27 remaining, and Piedmont held on for the 29-26 victory. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team traveled to Chabot College in Hayward for the 2023 Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament on Friday and Saturday, November 3-4. Tanya Kononova placed second after reaching the singles finals for the second year, Carolina Romanczuk finished fourth in singles, and Kate Jumper and Arianna Kortum finished fifth in doubles. Piedmont entered eight total players in the tournament; Cecilia DeFazio and Emma Eisemon earned the fourth seed and a firstround bye, but fell in three sets to Ava Taner and Ayla Acaoglu, 2-6, 7-6 (7-3), 11-9 in the second round with DeFazio hampered by an injury. “Tanya got to the finals before running into Polina. articles.text: With most players 16 or under, Chad Ironside’s Barca soccer team clinched the Under 19 league title with an emphatic 5-2 win over long-time rivals EBU Warrior-Wolves in Alameda on Sunday, November 5. The victory capped an unbeaten run to hold off the Montclair Stingers, the Panthers, the Falcons and the Phoenix. Training in near darkness at Alameda Point, the 22-strong squad built a cohesive work ethic and inclusive spirit that proved too much for their older opponents. Barca started brightly. A rampaging run by Harry McNulty set up Miles Kim for the opening goal, followed later in the first half by Elias Reed-Miguel finding the top corner of the net with a sweet strike from the top of the box. Always dangerous, the Wolves made it 2-1 after a goalmouth scramble. Barca struck back when Peter Murdock threaded a pass to Lucas Ironside for a 3-1 lead at the break. The game’s outcome seemed in the balance when the Wolves made it 3-2 just after the restart, but Piedmont found its rhythm and took control. Peter Murdock found the net on a breakaway and iced the game with an assist to Thomas Ero in the dying minutes, setting off jubilation on the Piedmont bench. Players and coaches of the Under-19 soccer league champions Barca. Pictured are: Coach Chad Ironside (left), Eli Hildebrand, William Steele, Bodie Ironside, Coach Aaron Murdock, Dean Olliphant, Sean McKee, Miles Kim, Elias Reed-Miguel, Ryan Wendel, Peter Murdock, Thomas Ero, Dorian Poole, Shane McNulty, Harry McNulty, Lucas Ironside, Kasper Jansson, Declan Murphy, Kian Ghaderi, Jacob Ingle, Rocco Doubrava (Bishop O’Dowd), Coach Neil McKee. Not pictured: Finian Caulfield, Cary Ward, Owen Udkow.

articles.text: An exhibition featuring over 20 pieces by local artist Bernice “Bingo” Bing (1936-1998) is on view now at San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum. Born in San Francisco’s Chinatown, Bing was a young artist among the city’s Beat Era art scene, creating works from the 1950’s on. Although she grew up in an orphanage and bounced between foster homes as a child, she was able to earn her B.F.A. and M.F.A. at the California School of Fine Arts (San Francisco Art Institute), where she studied alongside painter Elmer Bischoff and other greats. Her paintings and illustrations explore abstract expressionism and figuration as well as Zen calligraphy and Western abstraction. Bing only recently became recognized for her artworks, but was a fixture in the San Francisco art scene until her death in 1998. Into View: Bernice Bing is the first in an ongoing series of collection exhibitions at Asian Art Museum that highlight the work of under-recognized modern artists. articles.text: Opera review by Paul Hertelendy The latest sensation in opera is the unorthodox Omar, written by the polymath folksinger Rhiannon Giddens, winner of a Pulitzer, MacArthur “genius” award, and a Grammy. With co-composer Michael Abels, she turned out the multicultural drama, now staged at the San Francisco Opera. It is based on the true story of Omar ibn Sayyid, a 19th century African-Arab Islamic savant and author who had been forced into slavery and shipped off to bleak servitude in the cotton fields of America. The work is unique in opera annals, combining multiple cultures, languages and faiths. After a dark first act of capture and captivity, the work comes brilliantly to life in the second when Omar’s talents emerge as author and imam of divine inspiration. The music produces many threads, variously Afro-Arabian, NewWorld slave dance, jazz/blues and early Americana bordering on spiritual—what you can achieve with an unorthodox two-composer lineup, a new feature for the well-deserved operatic Pulitzer Prize. Above all, Omar dramatizes one of the little-known heroic tales of emerging America, known mostly for his voluminous writings (religious and otherwise) in the archives. In the end, the opera emphasizes the variety of cultures that made America great while dramatizing the times of slavery, both evil and cruel. The cast is almost entirely black, echoing Gershwin’s Porgy and Bess. For much of the show, the spark was slow in ignition, with voices more theatrical than truly operatic. But these too opened up to lustrous life in the triumphant finale that so many of us found moving, with Omar leading the the farthest corners. In a recurrent posthumous part, Omar’s mother Fatima was played tautly by mezzo Taylor Raven. Stage Director Kaneza Schaal held together this quasi-historical account sprawled over 10 scenes. Unforgettable was the stage design by Christopher Myers and Amy Rubin, with immense trees draped in white cloths, and countless bolts of stage-embracing fabric from above. Conducting the challenging score was John Kennedy. This is a multifaceted opera whose time is now, destined to continue playing on many stages in the U.S. and abroad. articles.text: San Francisco Opera is premiering the opera Omar, with performances at the War Memorial Opera House through November 21. Written by Rhiannon Giddens and Michael Abels, it won the Pulitzer Prize in music this year. Omar is inspired by the true story of Islamic scholar Omar ibn Said, who was taken from his home in West Africa in 1807 and sold into slavery in South Carolina. While enslaved for his entire life, he wrote a series of Arabic-language works on history and theology. Said eventually chronicled his life into an autobiography, which Giddens and Abels drew heavily from to create the opera. Giddens’ libretto includes West African kora, bluegrass, spirituals, folk music and jazz. The opera is sung in English and Arabic with English supertitles. Tenor Jamez McCorkle sings the title role, with Taylor Raven as Fatima, Daniel Okulitch as Johnson, Brittany Renee as Julie, and Norman Garr as Abdul, Omar’s Pulitzer prize-winning composer Rhiannon Giddens. brother. The opera premiered at the Spoleto Festival in Italy in 2022. The creative team behind Omar is choreographer Kiara Benn, set designer Amy Rubin, costume designers April M. Hickman and Micheline Russell-Brown, lighting designer Pablo Santiago and projection designer Joshua Higgason. One hour before every performance music scholar Michael Mohammed will present an overview of the opera. Following select performances of Omar on November 11, 15, 17 and 21, audience members are invited to stay for a post-show conversation with the singers and the creative team. To learn more and to purchase tickets, visit www.sfopera.com
articles.title: SF Opera presents Omar now through Nov. 21

articles.text: Tickets to San Francisco Ballet’s annual performances of Nutcracker are on sale now, with performances December 13-30. San Francisco Ballet was the first company in the United States to present an annual holiday Nutcracker. The holiday favorite includes more than 150 dancers accompanied by the Ballet Orchestra performing Tchaikovsky’s classic score. Ar tistic Director Helgi Tomasson’s Nutcracker originally premiered the ballet in 2004 and it follows the same basic formula nearly 20 years later. The story begins on a foggy Christmas Eve in 1915, with Drosselmeyer putting the finishing touches on a magical nutcracker doll. It’s his gift for the Stahlbaum family, who have invited him to join their holiday festivities. Customers drop by his shop for last-minute Christmas gifts and Drosselmeyer shows them toys and clocks. Later, outside the Stahlbaum house, as people hurry home to their Christmas revelries, Drosselmeyer arrives with his beautifully wrapped present. Scenic design is by Michael Yeargan, costume design is by Martin Pakledinaz, lighting design is by James F. Ingalls and projection design is by Wendall K. Harrington. Visit https://www.sfballet.org/ productions/nutcracker/ to learn more and to purchase tickets. San Francisco Ballet’s Nutcracker begins on December 13.

articles.text: Artist Michael Stehr, a Piedmont native, has unveiled his recent paintings in an exhibit, titled “Going the Distance – Depicting Space on a Two-Dimensional Plane”. The show is on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays through November 19. About Michael Stehr Michael received his degree in Art History from Stanford in 1991, where the focus of his study was on Michelangelo and the Italian Baroque period. articles.text: Achille Bocus, Musical Director of the San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra, will be the featured soloist this Saturday, November 11 at 5 pm. in the rarely performed Concerto for Mandolin in B flat by Neapolitan composer Giuseppe Giuliano (1720-1776) at Piedmont Center for the Arts. According to Bocus, “Giuliano was composing in the mid 1700s in Naples, featuring a relatively new classical string instrument at the time – the mandolin. We’re delighted to bring this work to our audiences, as it’s a fantastic example of the kind of classical period piece that followed the baroque period and foreshadowed to the later more complex work of Mozart, Haydn, Beethoven, and others.” Raised in Milan, Italy, Bocus studied mandolin, double bass, electric bass, composition and conducting. Following his studies he went on to play double bass with some of the finest symphonic, operatic and chamber music orchestras in Italy, performing throughout Europe. From 2005-2008 he was conductor of the Orchestra a Plettro Citta di Milano. He moved to the San Francisco Bay Area in 2009 and began teaching mandolin to students throughout the Bay Area with his “Il Tremolo” method, He created SF Mandolin Orchestra at that time. The Piedmont concert on November 11 will feature music from the late baroque and classical periods on a theme of “Napoli and the Revolution.” In addition to the Giuliano Concerto, the orchestra will perform: • Selections from Johann Sebastian Bach’s Art of the Fugue • Selections from Wolfgang Mozart’s London Notebook • Giovanni Battista Sammartini’s Sinfonia in G Major for String Orchestra The family-friendly concert will begin at 5:00 p.m. on Saturday, November 11. Admission is $20 general, $15 student/senior, and free for children 12 and under. Tickets may be purchased at the door, or at the Orchestra’s ticketing site: sfmandolin.square.site. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue. articles.text: Shailene Woodley in Adrift Before you watch Adrift, resist the temptation to learn anything about the story or the overwhelming events that frame act three. The narrative is, in retrospect, two stories. The first – and I’m imposing something that doesn’t exist in the film – is a love story between two kindred spirits, Tami Oldham (Shailene Woodley) and Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin), both in their twenties. The year is 1983. The place Tahiti. Tami, who left her home in San Diego out of high school, began to drift from port to port throughout the South Pacific, working odd jobs, crewing on boats and tourist ships. She is newly arrived in Tahiti when she meets New Zealander, Richard Sharp (Clafin),. He has just arrived on his trim 36-foot schooner, the Mayaluga. Almost immediately they begin a relationship, nurtured by the gorgeous beaches, long sails on Richard’s boat, strolls through outdoor marketplaces, all awash in color and easy-does-it people. Their world is kissed by soft trade winds gently blowing through. The two relish being together and their carefree lives, while sharing a world view that takes them far off the grid. Richard asks Tami to join him in his travels and they plan their sail from Tahiti to places east. But unexpectedly, Richard meets two fellow sailors from London who propose to hire him to sail their spectacular boat, with all the possible comforts available on a 45-foote from Tahiti to San Diego. The offer is sweetened with $10,000 and two first-class plane tickets back to Tahiti after the boat is delivered. The money, Tami and Richard conclude, could keep them sailing for at least a year, and so they decide to leave their boat in Tahiti and make the trip. And so begins act three, which is the most intense part of the film. This is a compellingly entertaining film, especially wellacted by Shailene Woodley who is most convincing, not only in her connection to Richard when they are in Tahiti, but her all-in performance in act three. Full disclosure: I love sailing movies. I love the idea of sails filled with wind and the absolute silence, other than the sound of halyards banging softly against the mast, or waves hitting the bow and sending up a welcoming spray that reaches the cockpit. I spent a lot of time doing all of the above on the San Francisco Bay, out by Alcatraz, and over by Tiburon, with Sausalito in the distance. But there is a caveat: blue water sailing is profoundly different and requires a sustained diligence that acknowledges the full measure of the sea and its power. Which Adrift graphically conveys. Know that you don’t ever need to have stepped topside on a teak deck to become lost in Adrift. It’s an amazing film. Adrift. Directed by Baltasar Kormakur. Starring Shailene Woodley and Richard Sharp. 2 hrs. Rated: PG-13. Released in 2018. Streaming on VUDU/hulu/ Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: One Day relies on a familiar Hollywood trope: two attractive young people meet, have a strong mutual attraction, one often denied or ignored. Their lives ebb and flow and occasionally intersect. They may spend quality time together, best buds of a sort. And yet, they are unwilling to speak truthfully to one another about feelings and chemistry that are evident to the audience but only hinted at by them. It’s a sturdy template, recent examples being Definitely, Maybe; Made of Honor; Love and Other Drugs; and Friends With Benefits. And not to forget the brilliant 1989 rom-com When Harry Met Sally. In the compelling One Day, on the eve of their 1988 graduation from Glasgow University, Emma Morley (Anne Hathaway) and Dexter Mayhew (Jim Sturgess), fueled by celebratory alcohol, fall into bed. They are, however, suddenly overwhelmed by their mutual awkwardness and so they scuttle the plan to consummate what is a budding acquaintance and agree to be friends – but friends without benefits. And so the film becomes episodic, capturing one day each year when they reconnect, always on July 15. Over two decades, through stop and start jobs and careers, they meet, sometimes with good cheer, sometimes in despair. But they manage to meet. This is the source of the film’s charm; however, it’s also the source of its greatest weakness. Because their relationship has no real narrative arc – they only share 20 days together in a span of 20 years – there is no strong sense of a growing intimacy, ad distinctly no sense of urgency. Their conversations are, because of the constraints of time, often truncated, elliptical, but always rich with possibilities. As individuals, Emma and Dexter are ever appealing. But as a couple, their relationship seems a bridge too far. And the moment of honesty in which they declare what they feel for each other, never quite seems to arrive. Or if it does, it is too brief. It’s what the audience has been waiting for: that singular July 15th day, however fragile, when they overcome their hesitations and insecurities and grab onto one another as if their lives depended on it. Instead the movie begins to feel like two decades of speed dating – in first gear. It is, of course, those wonderful, disjointed vignettes that lead to a final act that holds the promise of being a culmination. What occurs is stunning and unexpected and it will be up to the audience to decide whether it is manipulative and heavy handed or a compelling transition to a long denouement. One Day. Directed by Lorie Scherfig. Starring Anne Hathaway, Jim Sturgess, Patricia Clarkson. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2011. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. articles.text: A scene from Furious 7 It’s hard to believe but this behemoth of a franchise, Furious, parts 1-7, started some 14 year ago. That was well before sequels morphed into franchises, which have become a staple of most Hollywood studios. Producers and writers in the last decade have counted on audiences viewing one installment and almost instantly beginning to wait for the next. It’s the equivalent of those old Republic Studios Saturday afternoon matinees that treated young audiences to Indiana Jones-type adventures, always careful to interrupt the action just as the hero was in serious jeopardy (driving off a cliff while duking it out with the bad guys in the rear seat of a very large black Packard), The screen suddenly filled with the promise: “To Be Continued!” Fast and Furious 1 found a recipe that worked (who knew?) and kept right on going. Dominic Toretto (Vin Diesel) was the quintessential heavy. articles.text: Part 4 in a series In the Post’s ongoing search for filmmakers in Piedmont or with Piedmont roots, we discovered Piedmont resident Jessie Deeter, a highly accomplished documentary film producer. Her academic background includes a Masters in Journalism from U.C. Berkeley, and a separate Masters from Berkeley in International Studies with a Middle East focus. She has been producing, reporting, and shooting documentaries for more than two decades. Jessie got her start in documentary filmmaking as an associate producer working on different projects for Frontline and Frontline/World, the acclaimed PNS programs, and has also produced stories for Al Jazeera As a Fulbright scholar in Oman, Morocco, she began working on the documentary A Revolution in Four Seasons, about the Tunisian revolution during the Arab Spring. It is told from the perspective of two Tunisians with very different perspectives. It premiered at Hot Docs in 2016 and has since been screened worldwide. Deeter’s nominated and award-winning filmography is rich and varied. For example, working with Oscar-winning director, Alex Gibney, she produced the Emmy-nominated HBO documentary Out for Blood in Silicon Valley that told the story of Elizabeth Holmes, her meteoric rise and the scandalous fall of her company Theranos. The film premiered at Sundance in 2019. She co-directed and produced the chilling documentary Keep Quiet And Forgive, which tells the story of Amish survivors of sexual abuse. It was the recipient of ITVS’ Open Call funding in 2021 and is still in development. Deeter also produced the prescient Do You Trust This Computer? Released by Elon Musk, it explores the now timely issue of Artificial Intelligence. and can be viewed on Vimeo. Working with director Chris Paine, she produced two environmentally relevant documentaries, Who Killed the Electric Car? and the subsequent Revenge of the Electric Car. Both films examined the initial demise of the budding technology involved in the radical design changes required to transition vehicles from gasoline to rechargeable batteries, and its later unanticipated resurrection. Revenge debuted at the Tribeca Film Festival on New York and was aired by the PBS’ show Independent Lens in 2018. Relying on the zeitgeist of documentary filmmaking, Jessie produced the extraordinary Spark: A Burning Man Story that does a deep dive behind the scenes of the annual Burning Man Festival in the desert in Northern Nevada. It debuted at the SouthXSouthwest Film Festival in 2013 and later aired on Showtime. Deeter also produced the penetrating documentary Death By Fire that asks the question of whether the state of Texas executed an innocent man. Cameron Todd Willingham was convicted of deadly arson based on questionable investigative expertise and testimony. The film debuted on PBS’ 2010 Frontline season and has been aired several times since. Deeter is currently working on three documentaries: one on Bitcoin; a run-up to the Tokyo Olympics that will feature the equine horse sport of Eventing; and a documentary on Elon Musk. Peter Sohn, Pixar Also in our search for Piedmont filmmakers the name of the remarkable Peter Sohn rose to the top. He is an award-winning Pixar filmmaker, animator, and voice actor. He graduated from the California Institute of the Arts (CalArts), and briefly worked for Walt Disney and Warner Bros. Studios where he worked with director Brad Bird on the animated feature The Iron Giant. In 2000, Sohn joined Pixar Animation Studios, where he has contributed to a panoply of acclaimed film projects. Early on Sohn was involved Animator and voice actor Peter Sohn Documentarian Jessie Deeter in creating the much-praised animated features Finding Nemo, The Incredibles and WALL-E, and directed the short film Partly Cloudy that was included in the Animation Show of Shorts. He went on to voice the character Emile in the animated feature Ratatouille, as well as voicing Squishy in Monsters University and Sox in Lightyear. He also directed the films The Good Dinosaur and the recently released Elemental, which debuted at the Cannes Film Festival. It is clear that his filmography is extensive and varied. For example, he co-directed the English-language version of Ponyo with John Lasseter and Brad Lewis and contributed to the highly regarded animated features Inside Out, Finding Dory, Onward, Soul, Cars 3, Toy Story 4, Soul, Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse, and the anticipated Inside Out 2 and Elio. He was born in Brooklyn, N.Y. and is married to Anna Chambers whom he met at CalArts. They have two children. Why film? All of the above is testimony to the strong appeal of film and filmmaking, hence it is not by chance that the Piedmont Post includes weekly coverage of a spectrum of movies. For more than a century, the ever morphing technology of filmmaking – from grainy, flickering black and white silent images, to the extraordinary CGI-driven large screen representations in crisp colors and enhanced by Dolby surround sound – has found worldwide appeal. It’s a compelling, dynamic medium. And coming soon to a sofa near you is streaming. And not to forget A.I. Let’s face it, as a species we love to be told a story, both real and surreal. It’s it’s not a stretch to imagine our antecedents gathered around a warming fire listening to an elder tell a captivating, harrowing, or wonderfully embellished tale. And thus was born, with a cascade of stars filling an ancient sky, the promise of film.

articles.text: If you will soon be 65 and you don’t have health insurance through your employer or your spouse’s plan, you’ll need to start looking into Medicare – so you should know your options. And your first big choice will likely be whether to go with original Medicare or Medicare Advantage. Which is right for you? For starters, there’s no one “correct” answer for everyone. Your choice will depend on a variety of factors, including your own health care needs, financial situation, preference for a particular provider, and so on. In any case, you’ll need to know the basics of the two programs to even begin evaluating your options. Here’s a quick overview: Original Medicare Original Medicare includes Part A (hospital insurance) and Part B (medical insurance for doctor’s visits and covered preventive services). You pay about $165 per month for Part B (or possibly more, depending on your income level). You can then choose to add Part D, which covers prescription drugs, for about $40 per month and Medigap, which may cost between $150 - $250 per month to cover gaps in Parts A and B. You may also want to pay for private coverage for dental and vision care. Medicare Advantage Medicare Advantage, also known as Part C, is offered by private plans and essentially replaces Medicare Parts A, B and Medigap. Because you must stay enrolled in Medicare Part B with Medicare Advantage, you pay the same $165 per month as you would in Medicare (again, subject to additional charges for higher incomes). Some Medicare Advantage plans have no premiums, while others may charge up to about $60 per month. Most Medicare Advantage plans include prescription coverage and many also include dental and vision. It’s not always possible to make an apples-to-apples comparison of Original Medicare and Medicare Advantage. Generally speaking, if you have Original Medicare with Part D and Medigap, you could expect less restrictive networks, making it easier to see the doctors of your choice, and less restrictive coverage – that is, you might be less likely to need pre-authorization for certain services as you might with Medicare Advantage. Furthermore, unlike Medigap plans, Medicare Advantage plans are not standardized

articles.text: With the price of French Champagne and some American sparkling wines going through the roof, the world is in serious need of good sparkling wine that does not break the bank, especially when you are having a party that will require multiple bottles of wine. When it comes to good value in table wines, Argentina has always been a good place to look, especially for red wines. Know your Medicare options If you will soon be 65 and you don’t have health insurance through your employer or your spouse’s plan, you’ll need to start looking into Medicare – so you should know your options. And your first big choice will likely be whether to go with original Medicare or Medicare Advantage. Which is right for you? For starters, there’s no one “correct” answer for everyone. Your choice will depend on a variety of factors, including your own health care needs, financial situation, preference for a particular provider, and so on. In any case, you’ll need to know the basics of the two programs to even begin evaluating your options. Here’s a quick overview: Original Medicare Original Medicare includes Part A (hospital insurance) and Part B (medical insurance for doctor’s visits and covered preventive services). You pay about $165 per month for Part B (or possibly more, depending on your income level). You can then choose to add Part D, which covers prescription drugs, for about $40 per month and Medigap, which may cost between $150 - $250 per month to cover gaps in Parts A and B. You may also want to pay for private coverage for dental and vision care. Medicare Advantage Medicare Advantage, also known as Part C, is offered by private plans and essentially replaces Medicare Parts A, B and Medigap. Because you must stay enrolled in Medicare Part B with Medicare Advantage, you pay the same $165 per month as you would in Medicare (again, subject to additional charges for higher incomes). Some Medicare Advantage plans have no premiums, while others may charge up to about $60 per month. Most Medicare Advantage plans include prescription coverage and many also include dental and vision. It’s not always possible to make an apples-to-apples comparison of Original Medicare and Medicare Advantage. Generally speaking, if you have Original Medicare with Part D and Medigap, you could expect less restrictive networks, making it easier to see the doctors of your choice, and less restrictive coverage – that is, you might be less likely to need pre-authorization for certain services as you might with Medicare Advantage. Furthermore, unlike Medigap plans, Medicare Advantage plans are not standardized – there’s a great deal of variation in provider networks, drug coverage, premiums, deductibles, copays/coinsurance and out-of-pocket maximums. And some plans have reputations for denying claims. When you’re shopping around for Medicare Advantage plans, you may want to talk to your friends and relatives who have them. You might also ask your doctors about their office’s experience with different Advantage plans regarding coverage of treatments and prompt payment of claims. And you might want to visit www. medicare.gov/plan-compare for help in finding plans. (For other Medicare-related questions, you could contact your state’s State Health Insurance Assistance Program at www.shiphelp.org.) One last point to keep in mind: Each year, during the open enrollment period, which, in 2023, runs from October 15 through December 7, you can switch from Original Medicare and Medigap to Medicare Advantage, or vice versa. However, if you switch to Medicare Advantage, you may face limits and restrictions on returning to your Medigap plan, should you ever desire to do so. As you can see, choosing the right type of Medicare coverage will take some research and comparisons – so leave yourself enough time to make the selection that best fits your needs. articles.text: Nancy Lee Martz, a resident of Piedmont for 58 years, passed away peacefully at her home on Thursday, October 26, 2023. She was 88 years young. Nancy lived a full and colorful life surrounded by lifelong friends — contributing her time to different interests and hobbies, being an extraordinary wife, a fiercely loyal friend to all, and arguably the absolute greatest mom ever. Born on December 7, 1934, in Sacramento, she was the daughter of John and Dorothy Bagdanoff. An only child with a penchant for books and exploration, Nancy quickly realized that Sacramento was a jumping-off point to something bigger. After attending Sacramento State for two years, she transferred to the University of California at Berkeley in 1954 and soon thereafter became a proud member of the Sigma Kappa sorority. After graduating from Cal in 1956, Nancy moved to San Francisco and began working at the J. Walter Thompson advertising agency. Nancy’s roommate in San Francisco, Barbara Fox Roach, also of Piedmont and a lifelong friend, would play a pivotal role in Nancy’s life, introducing Nancy to her future husband, Charles Thomas Martz, Sr. of Westfield, New Jersey. Nancy and Tom became engaged less than a year after meeting and were married in Sacramento on November 12, 1960. After living in San Francisco and Los Angeles, the couple finally settled in Piedmont in 1965, where they would live for the remainder of their lives. Nancy and Tom became members at Claremont Country Club in 1971, where Nancy honed her tennis game and eventually, much to the surprise of Tom, became quite an accomplished golfer. In her golf career she had three holein-ones After making her first hole-in-one, she lost the ball on the next hole. Tom, ever the sportsman, explained to Nancy the significance of putting the hole-in-one ball on display in a case. The next time she made a hole in one, she merely handed him the ball without mentioning why. When asked, “What’s this?” Nancy replied with a smile, “I made sure not to lose the ball this time!” Nancy served as Captain of the Claremont Women Golfers, successfully played for Claremont Country Club’s East Bay Team Play team, and partnered with Tom to win four Mixed-4-Ball titles, to name just a few of her accomplishments. She loved golf and the incredible friendships she Nancy Martz died at home in Piedmont on October 26. She was 88. made through playing the game. Off the sports field, Nancy was an incredible cook. Her love of cooking and her ability to create thoughtful culinary presentations was the impetus to launch a successful catering business with her two partners, Diane Anderson and Linda Arellano. The business lasted over a decade. Her prized recipe collection is filled with very technical descriptions and precise instructions such as “a pinch of,” a “squoosh of,” and the ever-present “just a dash to taste.” One commitment close to Nancy’s heart was her volunteer work with the Oakland Museum’s White Elephant Sale. Nancy served on the Public Relations and Media Committee for several years and devoted hundreds of hours over decades to this highly successful annual event. Nancy also cherished being involved in various other clubs and groups, including the Hoe and Hope Garden Club, her book club, different bridge groups, the San Francisco Ballet, and the San Francisco Symphony. Nancy is survived by her son Kyle and daughter Jane. She will now be enjoying a family reunion in Heaven with her son Tom Jr. and her husband of 54 years, Tom Sr. The family expresses its deepest thanks to Nancy’s caregiver, Kalesita Leslie Tupou, who watched over her and loved her wholeheartedly. Leslie and her husband Petui Mailau also cared for Tom Sr. in his last months and should be regarded as earthly angels for their devotion to others, including the Martz family. A Celebration of Life will be held at a later date, with details to follow. In place of flowers, the family suggests making a memorial donation in her name to a charity of choice, and make a point of telling those close to you how much you love them.

articles.text: Armed robbery at Monticello & Park Way On Wednesday, November 1, at approximately 3:25 p.m. two Piedmont residents were victims of an armed robbery at the corner of Monticello Avenue and Park Way. The victims were traveling home by car and upon arriving at their residence, they were confronted by two men armed with handguns. The men brandished their weapons and demanded the victims’ wallets, phones, watches, and keys. The victims immediately complied and the suspects fled on Park Way toward Highland Avenue. The vehicle was later identified as a stolen 2016 Nissan Maxima. No one was injured and the suspect vehicle has not been recovered. Piedmont Police Department is working with neighboring agencies to collect more information and apprehend the suspects. “On a local level, we continue to bring in extra officers to provide an increased presence of police officers in our community,” said Police Captain Chris Monahan. “Our public safety cameras will be coming online soon to augment the ALPR cameras already in place. We continue to ask our community to report possible crime or suspicious activity and share any videos they have with us. Videos do help us with leads,” he confirmed. In the meantime, Monahan has reiterated his offer to make house calls in the area to discuss crime prevention. “Being located in a major metropolitan area, Piedmont continues to be a very safe place to live but is not immune to crime. Our CORE 4 crime prevention program continues to be full of good crime prevention techniques. In addition, if residents would like an officer to come to their home to discuss further crime prevention and reduction ideas, we are happy to make house calls.” Requests can be made to Capt. Monahan at cmonahan@piedmont.ca.gov, or by calling 510-420-3012. Police are still searching for a stolen 2016 Nissan Maxima used in an armed robbery on November 1.
